DID HE FORGET HIS 'ANTI-FREEZE'?
Dec 8th 1956 PAR 60461-2 (PNR-G)

DID HE FORGET HIS 'ANTI-FREEZE'?

Motorists! How are you at 'starting
from cold' (provided you've any petrol)?
Then perhaps you'd like a go at this
icicle-festooned car, which is
expected to start up within 30 seconds
during rigorous pre-production
freezing tests at the Austin Motor
Company's plant at Longbridge, Birmingham.
To make sure the model can stand up to
extremes of cold, it is left to 'soak'
for up to 48 hours in a huge
refrigeration chamber where the
temperature is lowered to 30 degrees below
zero Fahrenheit, 62 degrees of frost.
Technicians who work on the test car
enter the freezing chamber through an
air lock and wear special 'polar'
protective clothing.
Dec 8th 1956 PAR 60461-2 (PNR-G)

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION IN EVENING PAPERS
OF MONDAY, DEC. 10th

activity: placing the shell of a 15ft. Albacore boat into an oven for steam-heat baking.

te.text:
THEY'RE BAKING BOATS FOR MASS PRODUCTION
February 15th 1958 PAR 69070-2 (Wo-R)

THEY'RE BAKING BOATS FOR MASS PRODUCTION

As sailing fast gains popularity as a sport,
modern mass production methods derived from
those developed during the war for making
wooden aircraft are being applied to the
manufacture of boats at the Hamble, Hampshire,
factory of Fairey Marine Ltd., a subsidiary of
the Fairey Aviation Company.
The craft are 'hot-moulded' from planks of
wooden veneer, a method which eliminates the
old and laborious method of boat-building by
individual craftsmen.
The shell of each boat is composed of layers
of planks applied to a mould to form 'skins'
glued together. Each shell is baked by
steam heat up to 100 degrees Centigrade for
about half an hour. Then it is taken out of
the oven and removed from the mould.
The resulting boat, it is said, will last a
lifetime and is proof against all the normal
ills which affect boats built by other methods.
More than 1,000 boats were produced at Hamble
in 1957, ranging from 7ft. 6in. dinghies to the
26ft. Atalanta sailing cruiser.
Over one-third of the output is exported.
PICTURE SHOWS:- The shell of a 15ft. Albacore
craft being placed in the oven for baking
at Hamble.
February 15th 1958 PAR 69070-2 (Wo-R)

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION IN EVENING
PAPERS OF MONDAY, FEBRUARY 17th.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
18 FEB 1958
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

activity: the process of making metal castings from paper flong in book production

te.text:
ROPER               16.3.39

50 to 100,000 FULLY BOUND BOOKS PER WEEK.
Some of the largest Perfector printing
machines in Europe: Printing 64 pages on
each side of the sheet.
The copy from the author goes to Linotype
machines - they have a keyboard similar to
that of a typewriter - which transforms the
printed word into metal type. The type is
made up into a page form which has a
facsimile taken off it in paper flong,
from which the metal cast is produced.
Plates are assembled in special order on the
bed of the printing machine and after the
application of ink, the printed sheet is
produced.
The printed sheet goes through nearly half-
a dozen operations such as folding, gathering,
sewing and cutting, when it is transformed
into the bound copy sold to the public.
Real leather is used for the making of cases.
Real 22 carat gold is applied to the lettering.
[overtyped: Some of the]
Above is one of the machines used in the
Coplax process. Its object is to produce
the concave front, and the convex back and
hinge.
OPS.

activity: drillers of Allerston Forest cheer in triumph after a major natural gas strike on land

te.text:
BRITAIN’S richest strike
of natural gas on land
has been made 6,000ft.
below a Yorkshire forest. A
24-hour test produced 10mil-
lion cubic feet of gas —
enough to supply a large
town.
 “It is a mighty big find,” said
French-Canadian Floyd Des-
rosiers, leader of a team who have
been drilling day and night for
four months.
 He added jubilantly: “We will do
even better when we drill down
another 1,500ft.”
 The drill at Lockton,
near Scarborough, is the
sixth sunk in the area by
Home Oil of Canada, at a
cost of about £100,000.
 Managing director Wil-
liam Ogilvie said: “We
hope we have struck lucky
this time.”
 CAUTION
 And the Gas Council added
to the gusher excitement
yesterday when they an-
nounced that their North Sea
rig Mr. Louie, can produce
12million cubic feet a day.
 Last night there were opti-
mistic hopes that Britain
and the North Sea may be
floating on one gigantic gas
field.
 The full potential of the
Yorkshire well may be
known in about a month.
 Mr. Desrosiers warned:
“Until we sink one or two
more drill holes we shall
have to temper our joy and
enthusiasm with some degree
of caution.”
 But he added confidently:
“There has never been any-
thing like this on land in
Britain. It is its biggest kick
in 25 years’ prospecting.”
LUCKY STRIKE—and the drillers of Allerston Forest cheer in triumph
[Blue felt-tip pen scribbles crossing out text and marking the paper]

XML) INAUGURATION OF EUROPE'S LARGEST FORGING
PRESS FOR ALUMINIUM ALLOY

Europe's newest and largest forging press for aluminium
alloy was inaugurated yesterday at the Redditch (near
Birmingham) works of High Duty Alloys, Ltd., by the
Chairman, Sir Frank Spriggs. Known as "Goliath," this
12,000-ton press, the first of its type in Great
Britain, has been designed to give working pressure of
4,000, 8,000, and 12,000 tons. The press itself weighs
800 tons and has an overall height of 56ft. 4in. Of
this, 42ft. 9in. is above ground level and the remainder,
with the hydraulic system for operating the movable
table, is concealed below ground level. It cost more
than £500,000.

te.text:
MOBILE POWER UNIT FOR VENEZUELAN OILFIELDS

A complete electrical sub-station on wheels -
the first of its kind to be constructed in this
country - is now on its way to Venezuela for use
in Shell's oilfields around Lake Maracaibo. Being
easily mobile at short notice the sub-station will
augment or temporarily replace any of the existing
14 static sub-stations and can also be used to
provide a temporary supply to parts of the oil-
fields not served by permanent stations. The plant
and all necessary control gear are fixed and
cabled up on a towed 40-ton trailer, with acces-
sories carried in an accompanying truck. The
unit was constructed by Messrs. Parolle Electrical
Plant Co. Ltd. of Newcastle-upon-Tyne.

PICTURE SHOWS:-- The mobile power unit during a
three-hour test carried out in the Newcastle--
upon-Tyne area before dismantling and shipment.

PLEASE RETURN TO

te.text:
LONDON AS WORLD'S GEM INDUSTRY CENTRE?
August, 1945.
Experts who came to England from Holland and Belgium
in 1940, have established in London the business of
manufacture and export of gem diamonds. Exports have
already exceeded a million and a quarter pounds. These
pictures, taken at British Diamond Cutters works in
London, reveal a hive of industry, and there is room
for many more men. British ex-service men included,
to carry on the work. Many of the polishers and cutters
were refugees from Antwerp in 1940, others are ex-service
men who have proved highly skilled after most rapid
tuition. This firm alone exports up to £300,000 worth
of diamonds yearly. The picture shows:-

£12,000 worth of diamonds in various stages of
preparation from rough stones on left to finished
gems on right. In centre is a magnificent emerald
cut diamond worth £2,000. This stone in the rough
weighed 40 carats but cutting and polishing have
reduced it to 14 carats. (No. 6).

COPYRIGHT PHOTO ISSUED BY
CENTRAL PRESS PHOTOS LTD.
INCORPORATING
Central News Illustrations Service,
119, FLEET STREET, LONDON, E.C.4.

activity: Helicopter rescue of 45 crew members from the North Sea drilling rig Ocean Prince during a storm.

te.text:
Helicopt

A NORTH SEA drilling rig was
breaking up yesterday as a
helicopter pilot snatched the
crew of 45 to safety.
The £2 1/4 million rig Ocean Prince
was being battered by waves almost
60ft. high and winds gusting to
90 mph.
Captain Robert Balls carried out
his one-man rescue operation after
the rig's 136ft.-high drilling derrick,
radio room and two cranes had toppled
into the raging sea, and three of its
18 legs had collapsed.
The crew were marshalled at the
undamaged end of the 300ft. by 200ft.
rig to await Captain Balls's helicopter.
As the gale raged on, the Ocean
Prince, moored 110 miles east of Scar-
borough, bumped and bored furiously
against the sea bed. And
last night crewmen esti-
mated that a third of the
rig had fallen into the sea.
Some of the rescued men
were taken to the rig Con-
stellation, 20 miles away,
and some were flown to
land.
Last night a spokesman for
the owners, Burmah Oil Explo-
ration, said the men on Constel-
lation would stay the night
there because of the storm.
Captain Balls, 32-year-old
father of three, was called from
his bed in a Scarborough hotel
at 6am. after a Mayday signal
from the rig.
TRICKY
At 6.45 am. he took off from
a Scarborough helicopter pad.
He flew out to the rig and landed
in howling winds.
He picked up 19 men and
transferred them to the Con-
stellation after a tricky landing.
Then he flew back to Ocean
Prince to pick up 18 men, whom
he took back to Constellation.
Back he went to Ocean Prince
to pick up the remaining 8 men
and take them ashore.
He deliberately did not refuel
until the final stage of the
rescue because he was overload-
ing the helicopter and balancing
the extra weight by running low
on fuel.
Captain Balls, of Ashby-cum-
Fenby, near Grimsby, said later:

SECRETS OF THE CHINESE 
 IN THE KILNS OF CHEYNE ROW   DG/ PM 
 Visitors to the Loan Exhibition of 
 Chelsea China at the Royal Hospital, 
 Chelsea this month and next, will have 
 an opportunity to see some of the best work 
 of MR CHARLES VYSE the famous Chelsea potter. 
 The work on show is proof enough that the 
 Vyse kilns in Cheyne Row, are every bit as 
 productive as were those in Lawrence street 
 and Justice Walk in the heyday of the famous 
 Chelsea China factory over 200 years ago. 
 With his colleague Barbara Waller, Mr Vyse has 
 rediscovered the secret of the pottery of the 
 fabulous Chinese Sung Dynasty, a secret lost 
 to the Chinese long ago, and known nowhere 
 in Europe save in Cheyne Row. 
 PHOTO SHOWS:- BARBARA WALLER examines 
 the "May Queen" to see that her enamel 
 painting has fired up correctly 
 FOX PHOTOS  July 2 1951 44/433

activity: Members of the Mellor family re-thatching Maerdy Farm house and celebrating a 21st birthday.

te.text:
Stephens, Cardiff.  D.H.  2.11.56.
THATCHER 'ON THE TILES'
Thatching has been the work of the Mellor family
from Burton on Trent for generations. When their
father died nearly twenty years ago Harry Mellor
was faced with the task of carrying on the craft and
training his three younger brothers. Now the four
brothers travel all over the country, doing their
skilled work. This week, while three of them work
re-thatching Maerdy Farm house at Rumney, near
Cardiff, the youngest brother, Fred celebrated his
21st birthday. After he had carried the last load
of reeds up to his brothers Fred carried up his
celebration ale. He is the youngest craftsman in
the business, they think.
O.P.S. Fred Mellor takes a bundle of reeds to 25
year old William.

O.P.S. The brothers drink at toast. Top Harry (34)
William(25,) and Fred(21.)

FINALLY, Miss and Mr. Everyman.

basked under a

" This is likely

evening, I'm

measles, and that meant a hurried break-
fast—tea and toast and cereals—and a
visit from the doctor, and all the business
of the sickroom, and the job of keeping
Carol away from infection.
" Still, the evening's ahead, and isn't
spring good? "

activity: the Ferguson 35 de-luxe (Diesel Model) tractor

te.text:
ART LIBRARY
PLEASE RETURN
TO
DAILY HERALD
20 OCT 1956

E M B A R G O
NOT TO BE PUBLISHED BEFORE 4.00 p.m. ON MONDAY,
October 1st, 1956

NEW FERGUSON TRACTOR - the FERGUSON 35 de-luxe (Diesel Model)

The Ferguson 35 de-luxe incorporates numerous entirely new features
resulting from 13 years of intense research. The famous Ferguson hydraulic
system has been revolutionised. In addition to raising and lowering an
implement and automatically keeping a plough or cultivator at a selected
depth on uneven ground, the new hydraulic system gives the tractor driver
perfect control of front, mid or rear-mounted implements.

A new dual clutch gives a "live", engine-driven power-take-off for
power driven implements such as mowers or balers. A six speed gear box pro-
vides a wide selection of gears for every job on the farm enabling full use
to be made of the 37 brake h.p.. An alternative, ground speed p.t.o. in
hay making or fertilising, irrespective of the gear selected.

Among the many other important new features are included more
precise and easier steering, two steering brake pedals on the right hand
side of the transmission housing, a new safety starter, safety fuel tank,
instrument panel with a combined tachometer, speedometer and hour meter,
foamed cushion seat and padded back rest. Also new is the styling in two-tone
Ferguson grey and metallic bronze.

te.text:
16965I(CHI). NEW SHERVIK TRACTOR DEMONSTRATES EQUIPMENT
FOR USE IN EAST AFRICAN GROUNDNUTS SCHEME.

BAGSHOT(Surrey)ENG: A demonstration of the new Shervik
tractor, which has been specially designed for work on
the British Government's East African groundnut scheme,
was held near here. The new tractor, built by
Vickers-Armstrongs Ltd, combines certain of the components
of the Sherman Mark V tank, including one of the two-stroke
Diesel engines.
All the tractors are fitted with a universal "U" frame
to which a variety of implements can be fitted. Stumper
blades are used for digging out tree stumps with their
roots, and trees can be quickly uprooted by the use of
the treedozer. After the root-cutter has been at work
collection of the roots is accomplished with a rootrake,
16 feet in width.
"PHOTO SHOWS: - A Shervik tractor easily pushing down a
tree with the use of the treedozer, during the demonstration.

activity: manufacture and transportation of aluminium prefabricated bungalows from factory to residential site

te.text:
BIRTH OF
A PREFAB.
CONVOY
They are putting up alu-
minium bungalow No. 6886
at Ockenden, Essex, where it
will provide a home for
someone on a waiting list.
From the other side of
England, a "Herald" re-
porter tells how he saw No.
6886 come off the assembly
line to swell the Homes Con-
voy.
MOTORING to the Bristol
Aeroplane Company's fac-
tory at Oldmixon, near Wes-
ton-super-Mare, I passed 15
"Homes Convoy" lorries in as
many minutes—carrying sec-
tions of aluminium bungalows
to all parts of the South.
9½ in a minute
It is just over two years since
Airoh bungalow No. 1 left this
factory, which produced Beau-
fighters during the war. Today
these cream and green prefabs are
leaving Oldmixon at the rate of 30
a day from the conveyor belt
where No. 6886 was born.
"Life" for No. 6886 started on
Thursday at 8 a.m. when its floors,
in four sections,
were con-
structed in Old
Nixon's No. 7
workshop. Later
in the day the
floors were
moved by over-
head crane to
the conveyor
belt for assem-
bly of kitchen
and bathroom units.
Moved by tractor to No. 8 work-
shop, No. 6886 acquired its walls,
windows, doors, and roof as its
four parts moved 9½ inches a
minute down the assembly lines.
On Friday, at 7.45 a.m., No. 6886
was about to enter the factory's
huge paint-spraying tunnel, where
the paint is treated with hot and
cold air.
At 10.15 it was driven out of the
factory
And at 3 p.m. it left the factory
gates—less than 20 hours after its
first part was assembled.
I talked to the four drivers
taking No. 6886 to Ockenden—an
11½ hours run. Ex-RAF "Erk"
Roy Shingfield said: "When
I drive along with a part of one
of these houses I think: 'Some
lucky one has got a home to live
in.'"
Roy is hoping to get married
next year, if he can get a house.

THIS PRINT IS THE
PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED
UNDAMAGED.

te.text:
Master Caption for Two Photos

From:   Seager, Evans & Co.,
        20 Queen Anne's Gate,
        London, S.W.1.

                                  For release -
                                  1 p.m. October 7th, 1960.
Contact: R. A. Wright
         WHItehall 5067

DISTINGUISHED FIRST -- First whisky distillery to be built in
the Speyside area of the Scottish Highlands in the 20th century
(Photo No. 1) was formally opened today (October 7th) by Long John
Distilleries, Ltd.  Located at Tormore-on-Speyside, Morayshire,
the plant can produce 300,000 proof gallons of malt whisky a year
and work already is underway to expand the distillery's capacity
another 100,000 gallons.

Key workers (mashmen, stillmen, plant managers) live in rent-free,
five-room houses (Photo No. 2) ranging in value from £3,500 to
£7,000.  They were built by Long John on a 40-acre tract adjacent
to the plant.  Supplies of meat, produce, baked goods and other
necessities are brought to the village daily by "mobile" shops.

te.text:
AIMED AT THE EXPORT TARGET: 
BOWS OF STEEL ARROWS OF ALUMINIUM    DG/HT

     If Robin Hood and his Merry Men  could return
to their legendary haunts under the Greenwood Tree,
they would be surprised to find that  their stout
yew bows  had been superseded by superior weapons
of the finest steel.  Arrows too, are no longer the
grey goose feathered shafts   which routed the French
at Agincourt.    The bowman of 1950 uses aluminium.
     With the export market  as their target, a well
known steel tubing firm in Birmingham (Messrs. Accles
and Pollock) are now making  the new  bows and arrows
in steel and aluminium.  The steel  long bows are
said by expert archers, to give   far better performance
and greater accuracy than wooden weapons. Orders for
them  have  been coming in from all parts of the world.
     Making the bows, involves 200 processes, almost
everyone byhand. Fourteen heat treatments   are needed
and the  thickness of the tapered steel tube from which
the bow is drawn has to be controlled within one-thousandth
of an inch.

PHOTO SHOWS:- "Bow-belle". This young lady is putting
the crest on the aluminium arrows at the factory, before
they are exported.

FOX PHOTOS   Jan 22nd 1950 413237

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
23 JAN 1950
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

COPYRIGHT
FOX PHOTOS
DUPLICATE SENT MANCHESTER
CENT. 7831

FUEL SHORTAGE CAUSES AUSTIN SHUT-DOWN: THOUSANDS OUT.

All production employees of the Austin Motor Company's works -
14,800 in all - are affected by a shut-down of the factories caused

will be impossible to start work again unless the present allocation
is revised and delivery increased, and the works may be closed for
several weeks.

plants throughout Britain have had to close down temporarily, and many
thousands of workers have been thrown out of work.

activity: A specially-shaped fruit picking ladder in the course of construction at the Dean Forest Rural Industry workshop.

te.text:
INDUSTRY IN THE FOREST
RURAL CRAFTSMEN   IN THE FOREST OF DEAN

DG/MAE

The growth of agriculture has brought more work to
the rural craftsmen who make farm requisites such
as fencing, hurdles, tools and ladders. Fruit picking
ladders of special design is the speciality of the
Dean Forest Rural Industry, at Longhope in the
Forest of Dean .    The ladders have a wide splay at
the base and  as well as being much favoured locally,
they are rapidly becoming popular all over the country.
  The workshop in the Forest  also turns out large 
quantities  of sheep hurdles and fencing, and thousands
of tent pegs-most of the latter for the export market.

PHOTO SHOWS: "Steps in craftsmanship". A specially-shaped
fruit picking ladder in the course of construction,
at the Rural Industry workshop. in the Forest of 
Dean . Note the wide base.

activity: a member of the Women's Land Army cutting a forked twig from a hazel tree to use for water divining

te.text:
ESTEN                                  ILLUS.                  10.6.42
LAND GIRL DISCOVERED AS WATER DIVINER.
It has taken the Women's Land Army to find out
that Miss Littler, a volunteer in the employment
of the Flintshire War Agricultural Executive
Committee possesses the gift of water divining.
Miss Littler joined the Women's Land Army March 1941
and is one of 9 girls employed on gang work.
Recently they were working on a piece of land which
was constantly being flooded by a hidden spring.
Mr.J.T.Richards, the Executive Officer of the
Flintshire War Agricultural Executive Committee, had
made extensive efforts to have the spring located.
Finally, he asked the 9 members of the Women's Land
Army, who were clearing the land, to try with a
hazel stick to see if they could divine this spring.
Miss Littler was found to be the only one who
possesses this unusual gift.
Since Flintshire farmers have heard of this there
have been many requests for her services, to help
in reclaiming flooded land and so save hundreds
of pounds in drainage. Also farmers wish to use
her to help to discover water for sinking wells.
O.P.S.1.  The first step to becoming a Diviner
is to cut a forked twig from a hazel tree.
Miss Littler who is 19 years of age is seen on
right.

activity: crowds gather outside the St Stephen's entrance of the House of Commons demanding equal pay for men and women in the Civil Service

te.text:
Last night outside the House of Commons as police close St. Stephen's entrance against the huge crowd trying to get to the Lobbies.
HERALD REPORTER
THE girl from behind the Post Office counter, the little lady who types those polite demands "Dear Sir, unless ..." and 3,000 other women from Government offices packed Central Hall, Westminster last night. 
With one voice they declared: "We want equal pay." A smattering of men came along to back them.
Mr. Hugh Gaitskell, Chancellor of the Exchequer, has already said the Government accepts the principal, but that nothing can be done about it at this critical period, as it would have a serious inflationary affect.

217405 OCK.

LONDON: Demanding equal pay for men and women
in the Civil Service, crowds gather outside
the St Stephen's entrance of the House of
Commons after a meeting at the Central Hall
Westminster, shouting "We want Gaitskell"....

activity: Completed working class houses at the St Paul's Cray estate.

te.text:
ESTATE FOR ALL INCOMES.
First turf on the site of a London County Council community estate, to cater for higher as well as lower income groups, was cut by Mr.I.J. Hayward, a leader of the L.C.C.
The 72 "middle income" houses included in the St Paul's Cray estate will be built in pairs, each with a garden back and front, a drive and garage.
Downstairs there will be a hall, cloakroom, large sittingroom and lounge separated by sliding doors, dining room and modern kitchen.
Upstairs will be four large bedrooms and bathroom.
The houses will be let at an economic rent of between £130 and £150 a year, exclusive of rates.
The 570 acre estate will have 3,883 dwellings altogether and include three-storey blocks of flats, five modern schools, churches, shops, a cinema, public-house, parks and a large playground. It will cost £5,500,000.
OPS. Two of the completed working class houses which will be ready for occupation in October.

activity: The Queen signing the Sentence of Consecration at the new Cathedral Church of St. Michael.

te.text:
THE Consecration
of the new
Cathedral Church
of St. Michael here
today was a cere-
money of simple,
yet luxurious
beauty.
The simplicity was in
the small, central acts
of consecration; the
luxury was in the
splendour of the set-
ting, the richness of
the ritual.
AWE
There were first the
processions, 11 of them in
all, containing a Queen, a
Princess, nine arch-
bishops, a stiffening of
knights, innumerable am-
bassadors.
Last but one came the
Queen's procession, pre-
ceded by her Gentlemen-
at-Arms, those clinking,
grey old gentlemen who
supply these occasions
with a sort of instant awe.
YELLOW
The Queen, in yellow,
was received at the gate
of the old cathedral by
the Bishop of Coventry,
Dr. Cuthbert Bardsley,
and escorted to the west
door of the new.
In her procession
walked Sir Basil Spence,
the Cathedral architect.
Fanfares, drums, and
then, as they died down,
the business of consecra-
tion. A technical cere-
mony, which begins,
superbly, with the Bishop
shouting "Open the
door."
The small unconcealing
glass doors swing open
and the Bishop, hitherto
seen but unheard, is es-
corted in.

The Queen signs the Sentence of Consecration. Her name as first wit-
ness is followed by that of the Archbishop of Canterbury, Dr. Ramsey.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
26 MAY 1962
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

activity: The upstream face of Clunie dam, now nearly completed.

te.text:
HIGHLAND POWER SCHEME NEARLY READY
Cpr. 25.10.49.
The North of Scotland Hydro-Electric Board's Tummel-Garry
scheme, is expected to go into operation at the end of this
year when parts of the Clunie dam are completed. The 386 foot
long and 65 foot high Clunie dam at the Eastern end of Loch
Tummel will raise the level of the Loch by 17 feet and
more than double its length. The water will flow through a
23 foot diameter tunnel for two miles to the Clunie Power
Station, where three turbo-alternators with a total capacity
of 57,000kws, will be in operation. To equalise the fluctuating
discharge from Clunie Power Station will be the primary
function of the 480 foot long 74 foot high dam at Pitlochry.
Here, the power station is incorporated in the dam, and two turbo-
alternators will have a generating capacity of 15,000 kws.
Both dams have a fish ladder to enable salmon to reach the
upper reaches of the River Tummel. The whole scheme will have
an annual output of about 300 million units, and will have
another dam on the upper reaches of the River Errochty which
will have a high water level nearly 1,100 feet above sea-
level. The picture shows:-

No.1. The upstream face of Clunie dam, now nearly completed.
The concrete structure has been painted black to forestall any
action of the peaty water, and to seal any minute cracks in the
face of the wall. Note the tiny figure of a workman half-way
up the face [illegible] on the right hand side.

COPYRIGHT PHOTO ISSUED BY
CENTRAL PRESS PHOTOS LTD.
119, FLEET STREET, LONDON, E.C.4
CENTRAL 2266/7.

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF
'DAILY HERALD' AND MUST BE
RETURNED TO THE ART LIBRARY BY
JAN 20 1950
Indus Fuel & Power - Electr - Water Power.

te.text:
NEW STEEL FROM THE SCRAP HEAP.    AW/AT

There is now a tremendous demand for scrap metal, which is
fetching a good price. These pictures were taken at a
Letchworth foundry where scrap steel is analysed on arrival
and the best quality cut into short lengths with oxy-acetelene
flames. It is then fed into cupolas where it becomes molten
iron. This iron is then transformed into high quality steel
by a battery of "converters" and turned into anything from
an engine wheel to a ship's davit.

melting in the cupolas.

LN 269016      TEA        LONDON BUREAU
BUILD THEIR OWN HOMES IN SPARE TIME.

LONDON: Clerks, builders, printing workers and
lorry drivers are among the 25 members of the
Camberwell Enterprise Housing Club, who are
building their own homes on a site at Crystal
Palace (South London). The idea was born two
years ago, now every night, and at weekends
and holidays, the men work on the houses.
Neighbours lend a hand and much of the work
is done at night with the aid of floodlights.
Special features of the homes will be a modified
form of central heating; a garage to each house;
and a new "Accotile" plastic tile flooring
throughout. Skilled, unpaid foreman is Bill
Clark, who with Len King, a building representative
during the day, works in the "site" hut with the
plans. Bill will be the first to move into one
of the new homes - in May. The project is expected
to be completed in two years time.
PHOTO SHOWS: LEN KING - a building representative
in the daytime - tests the door jambs of one of
the houses. REG BRUCE, a paint worker, and HARRY OTT
(right), a printer, lay bricks.

activity: Residents in the open-plan and fenced gardens of a housing development.

te.text:
HOW would you like to move into a new luxury £4,600 home without a lawn of your own, a front gate or a fence to gossip over?
Open-plan houses like this are already a common feature of suburban life in America, Canada and Australia; on a smaller scale, they are also found on council estates in Britain.
But now, because of the high cost of land on private developments, "togetherness" living is spreading among the young families who are buying a brand new home of their own.
Castles
If you live on one of these estates, you share the expenses of a gardener to mow the communal lawn, the upkeep of service roads, shared drive-ins and planned gardens.
Traditionally, we British like our "castles." We fence ourselves in and keep the neighbours out with a privet hedge and a stout front gate.
But the old attitude is already changing in the face of the high cost of seclusion on the new building developments. Damer Gardens in Henley-on-Thames, Oxfordshire, is typical of these new developments.
Back gardens are divided by post and rail fences, though some residents are already reinforcing these with barriers of wattle.

activity: Exploratory oil drilling in Lancashire, showing mud circulation from deep bore holes.

te.text:
DcH White 13/7/49
Oil search at Formby
8/ Sam Bromley watches mud circulating
from 216 ft below ground being brought
up to surface

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNREPAIRED.

SEARCH FOR OIL IN LANCASHIRE.
Somewhere beneath the sand-dunes of the Lancashire
coast, seven miles from Southport, lies a huge
untapped supply of oil.
Sixteen engineers who have just sunk a bore hole hope
to find it before their instruments register 7,500 ft.
They cannot go any deeper than that with their present
equipment and if they have not found it at that depth
they will try somewhere else.
An official at the D'Arcy Exploration Co, who is doing
the work, said "for ten years we have been getting 400
tons of oil a year from eight 'surface wells' at
Formby, but those wells are only 100 ft deep and we are
confident that a large oilfield, much deeper is
supplying them".
They tried three times before at Scarisbrick and
Bickerstaffe, but although they went down to 7,600 ft
they could not find the source.
Pointing to a thick, pinky fluid oozing out of a large
pipe alongside the towering derrick on the new site,
John Gibson the drilling superintendant explained
"that is the circulating mud which we pour down the
centre of the drill pipe, It seeps through the drilling
bit and brings up the small pieces of rock formation".
After the formation has been sieved out, the mud goes
back down the drill pipe.

te.text:
FIRST STAGE OF BLACKWALL TUNNEL DUPLICATION SCHEME.
21.4.58
London E.1.
Road work in connection with the London County Council's
scheme for the improvement of the Northern approach
to the Blackwall Tunnel-the first stage of the project
for the duplication of the Tunnel-began today. Mr
A.A. Nugent, Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Transport, started the work on the site, bounded by
East India Dock Road, Brusnwick Road, Drew Street and
St Leonards Road, today. The total cost of the improvements
is estimated at £1,600,000- including road works,
aquisition of property and rehousing of displaced families.
It is expected that the work will be completed by the end
of 1960.

I.N.P. PHOTO SHOWS: Mr A.A. Nugent, Parliamentary Secretary
to the Ministry of Transport, is instructed in
driving a Bulldozer by Mr Hughie Gallagher,
when he started the work on the site today.
Picture by Monte Fresco Jnr.
TDH/122883 INTERNATIONAL NEWS PHOTOS.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
22 APR 1958

TO

THE SILVER UNDERGROUND: 
 ATTRACTS U.S. BUYERS 
 DG/RS 
 
 When the premises of many antique silver 
 dealers in Chancery Lane were bombed during 
 the war, they literally went "underground". 
 The large strong rooms below ground in a 
 blitzed safe deposit building became "shops" 
 for the dealers to display their valuable 
 wares and an antique silver market below ground, 
 has sprung up. Many U.S. and Canadian buyers 
 spend large sums of money at the "underground 
 silver market".

activity: Labourers hand-sowing barley seed at Tillingdown Farm during the spring battle for harvest.

te.text:
BROADCASTING THE SPRING SEED........
BATTLE FOR THE HARVEST BEGINS IN BRITAIN.

With the first few sunny days of Spring sunshine, farmers
all over Britain are ploughing and sowing with all speed to gain
the valuable time lost through floods and tempest throughout the
land..   More than six weeks have been lost through severe
Winter weather, and the farmers and their labourers toil from
dawn till dusk in the great battle for the harvest - sorely needed -
which is to follow their present efforts.
Down on Sir Peter Greenwell's estate at Caterham, Surrey, the
ground, still heavy with moisture, would not be ready for sowing
by mechanical means for several days to come - but time is precious
and the sowing is being done by hand to gain valuable hours........
PHOTO SHOWS:- Scattering the seed.   Labourers broadcasting barley
seed by hand at Tillingdown Farm, Caterham, Surrey.
Caterham village can be seen in background.
DAW.                 13th April, 1947.          PN-s.

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

COPYRIGHT
PLANET NEWS LTD
3, JOHNSON'S COURT,
LONDON, E.C.4

16.12.60.
PREVIEW OF BRANDON ESTATE, SOUTHWARK.
TO BE OPENED TOMORROW.

Brandon Estate, Southwark, a major L.C.C.
project combining the rehabilitation of nearly 200
old houses with the provision of over 1,000 new
dwellings ranging from old persons' bungalows to
18-storey point blocks, will be opened tomorrow (Dec.
17) by the Chairman of the L.C.C. (Mrs. F.E. Cayford).
The estate is one of the largest of the L.C.C.'s
redevelopment schemes for inner London, and is the
first example of the L.C.C.'s policy of infusing new
life into decaying areas of London's "middle belt"
by combining the complete redevelopment of the property
in worst condition with thorough modernisation of
property still in sound structural order. There is
accommodation for 5,000 people, and the estimated total
cost of the work is £3,596,450.

KEYSTONE PHOTO SHOWS:- Interior view showing
the [struck through] living room in the flat occupied
by Mr. and Mrs. Lewington - at today's preview
of the estate.

H/Keystone EM/725097

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
17 DEC 1960
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

22ND. SEPT.
PURE FOODS CONFERENCE.

AS PART OF THE CELEBRATIONS OF THE CENTENARY
OF THE FIRST PURE FOOD LAW PASSED BY THE
BRITISH PARLIAMENT, DELEGATES FROM THE
COMMEMORATIVE CONFERENCE BEING HELD THIS
WEEK IN LONDON VISITED THE HAYES CHOCOLATE
FACTORY OF THE NESTLE COMPANY LIMITED TODAY.

THEY WERE MET BY THE MANAGING DIRECTOR,
MR. F.A. KIRBY, AND THE FACTORY MANAGER,
MR. K.V. SANDERSON, WHO ACCOMPANIED THEM ON
THEIR TOUR.

THE DELEGATES SHOWED A SPECIAL INTEREST
IN THE ATTENTION GIVEN TO CLEANLINESS AT
THE HAYES FACTORY, AND THE HIGH STANDARD
OF QUALITY CONTROL OF ALL THE COMPANY'S
PRODUCTS.
THE VISITORS ALSO MET MR. M.H. BREWER,
CHIEF CHEMIST, AND MR. T.G. MORRIS, MARKETING
MANAGER (CHOCOLATE).

PICTURE SHOWS:- THE VISITORS SHOWED A KEEN
INTEREST IN THE CONFECTIONERY PRODUCTION
LINES. ON THE LEFT OF OUR PICTURE, NESTLE'S
CHIEF CHEMIST, MR. M.H. BREWER EXPLAINS A
POINT TO ONE OF THE DELEGATES.

A ND here, miller Gwyn Bloom feels the texture of newly-
ground wheat flour by running it through his hands.

STEPHENS. CARDIFF.          31/3/54.
FLOUR MILL RE-OPENED.
When the flour mill on the banks of the
Teifi at Cenarth was closed at the start
of the war, most people thought that its
days were ended.
But now that wheat has been de-controlled
the mill has been overhauled and is once
more producing whole-meal flour for making
into bread that is in great demand in
the local bakehouses.
OPS. Mr. Gwyn Bloom, who was the miller
before the war, and who works there
occasionally now, watches the wholemeal
flour pouring once again from the stones.

3 5/8" wide x 4" deep
Welsh slip p. 7

te.text:
ENGINEERING JILL IMPROVES THEIR SKILL
October 30th 1968 PAP 136427-1 (PNR/P-D)

============================================

ENGINEERING JILL IMPROVES THEIR SKILL

     The best way , it would seem, to spur
on engineering apprentices to greater
effort, is to put a girl among the boys.
You can't stop them stealing admiring
glances at BARBARA HAMPSON, 18, -  she is
herself an apprentice at a Huddersfield
engineering company - but the 16 boy
apprentices work harder than ever. They
are determined not to be outdone in their
engineering skills by a member of the
opposite sex.
     The senior instructor at the school,
Mr. Brian Glendinning, declares that
Huddersfield's only girl engineering
apprentice is really keeping the boys
on their toes and, with a girl around
there is no bad language , even when a
boy drops a spanner on his toe.
     Barbara joined the firm from school,
after obtaining six G.C.E. "O" Levels,
including one for metalwork and another
for technical drawing. She wants to
become a draughtsman one day and said "I was
a bit worried at first among so many boys.
They tease me unmercifully but I'm getting
used to it".
October 30th 1968 PAP 136427-1 (PNR/P-D)

activity: unloading raw rubber bales from the ship 'Benlawers' onto a barge at Tilbury Docks

te.text:
FIRST POST-WAR CARGOES OF RAW RUBBER ARRIVE IN ENGLAND.

The first raw rubber cargoes to reach this country from Malaya for
nearly four years are being discharged in London docks. At Tilbury
Dock a cargo of about 580 tons of rubber has been unloaded from
the "Benlawers" - a transhipment from Singapore, picked up at
Calcutta. It is the second shipment to be made by the Rubber Control
buying unit.  The first, a small shipment of 150 tons which was
brought by the "Almanzora" to Southampton, was held up by the
dockers' strike and finally reached London by rail. A third
consignment of 300 tons from Singapore was brought into Liverpool
by the "Clan Chisholm". A fourth - and much larger - rubber cargo
of 8,300 tons left Singapore on board the "Empire" on October 28th.
PHOTO SHOWS:- A cargo of raw rubber from Malaya being unloaded
from the "Benlawers" onto a barge at Tilbury Docks, Essex: the
bales of rubber, which weigh about 280 lbs. apiece, are swung
overboard in nets, and manoeuvred into place on the barge.
DAV 21 November 1945 PN

COPYRIGHT
PLANET NEWS LTD.
3 JOHNSON'S COURT,
FLEET STREET, E.C.4.
PHONE: CENTRAL 3671-3

FIRST 8-STOREY LCC FLATS OPENED TODAY

Needwood House, Woodberry Down Estate, Stoke Newington -
the first eight-storey block of flats erected by the

te.text:
BERKSHIRE.

THE THATCHERS ARE BUSY.

In the quiet villages of Berkshire and Wiltshire the
thatchers are busy carrying out spring repairs on
farms and cots and age-old barns. There are plenty of
thatched roofs in this part of England and there is no
lack of work for the craftsmen in villages where sometimes
nearly every other roof is a thatch.

Photo shows- Mr. Adams and his son at work on a thatched
roof at Shrivenham which shelters half a dozen homes. It
has more than 6,200 square feet of thatch and seven tons
of straw were used on it. Mr. Adams is a busy man these days.
Fox April 2nd. 36.

SPRING THATCHING
Thatchers at work on a picturesque row
of cottages at Shrivenham, Berks. The
last few years have seen a welcome
revival in this rural industry, which at-
one time seemed in danger of dying out.

SWORDS FOR THE CORONATION.         AW/HT

The day of the sword as a weapon of war is over, but
swords are still used in the services for parades and
ceremonial occasions.  Swords for officers and high
personages and members of Diplomatic Corps who will
be taking part in the forthcoming Coronation ceremonies
are now being prepared by the Wilkinson Sword Company
of Chiswick, who have been making swords since 1772.
Most swords are engraved with a Service badge with the
King's initials forming part of the design on the King's
cipher.

Photo shows:-   Tom Beasley, a steel craftsman, wearing
the hat of the sword forger, seen forging a sword at
Chiswick.
Fox Jany 15th. 37.

NURSERY LANE SITE - HALLAMSHIRE HOUSES

Councillor Albert King, leader of the Leeds City Council, opened the first 40
factory built houses to be built on the Nursery Lane site at Moortown; more than
230 industrialised dwellings of various types are planned in the city during 1963-
64 and more than 500 in 1964-65.

These houses represent a transition between traditional construction and a fully
prefabricated system as being investigated by the Yorkshire Development Group.
(Founder members are Leeds, Sheffield and Hull, new members - Nottingham and
Scunthorpe. The group hope to speed-up and reduce the costs of municipal house
building by using industrialised methods of construction). Forty houses are
being erected in terraces on this site.

The houses are of the five-person three-bedroomed type and above the 'Parker
Morris' minimum standards as described in the Ministry of Housing and Local Govern-
ment's publication 'Homes for Today and Tomorrow'.

title: A photographic print of Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip, Visit to Newport, October, 1962

date_info.rationale: Stamps likely indicate processing or publication date.

activity: The Queen opening the Richard Thomas and Baldwin's steelworks at Llanwern.

te.text:
PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
27 OCT 1962
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

BY BASIL MORGAN
THE Queen pressed a small brass button yesterday—and set moving the giant rollers of Britain's most modern steelworks.
Then she watched the first 10-ton ingot start a spectacular half-mile journey to end up as a steel strip 100 yards long.
She was opening Richard Thomas and Baldwin's new £150million steelworks at Llanwern, near Newport, Monmouthshire.
It was a ceremony that nearly did not take place.
On Thursday night, an electrical fault put the whole chain of hot steel rollers out of action.
PUT RIGHT
An emergency squad of repair men worked through the night and on into the morning. They put the fault right only hours before the Queen arrived.
Later the Queen, who was accompanied by Prince Philip, saw the steelworks' computor room, where all processes are automatically tracked.
She took over one set of controls and altered the thickness of sheet steel being made for Jaguar cars.
From Hot Mills to High Jinks — that's the name of a five-year-old pony the Queen has bought for Princess Anne. An announcement last night said that the pony has already been delivered to the Royal Stables.

activity: Inspection of Royal Air Force Guard of Honour swords.

te.text:
THE RETURN OF THE SWORD

Coronation Brings It Back to Popularity

The sword, ancient weapon of defence, has now
become a token of ceremony. It will be much in
evidence during the Coronation festivities.
Many sword cutlers have gone out of business
in this age of the atom, but one firm, The
Wilkinson Sword Company, of Acton, London, have
kept up the ancient industry. At present they
have orders for 2,000 swords. They are busy making
officers' ceremonial swords or refurbishing old ones
that will be used in the Coronation.
Some of the orders received have come from Overseas.
The firm has the market largely to itself
- even American manufacturers appear to have
gone out of business.
Ceremonial swords have not been a standard item
of officers' equipment in the Army since before the
war. Many orders have been placed by the Ministry
of Supply and service-owned swords are issued to
officers as required from a pool formed by
regiments. Nevertheless, many officers still possess
pre-war swords and hundreds of these have been
sent for renovation, which mostly involves
replating. The average cost of this work is about
£5.
Many existing swords, including those belonging
to the Yeomen of the Guard, are being sent to the
firm to be brought up to date and embossed
with the Queen's cipher.

I.N.P. PHOTO SHOWS:- Long line of Royal Air Force
Guard of Honour swords are laid out for
final inspection by Mrs Anne Bourchier, of
Chiswick, (left) and Mrs. Doris Spenceley of
Shepherds Bush.

YOUNG DUTCH CRAFTSMAN AT

At the Rye Potteries (Rye, Sussex) many youngsters
are employed, in an effort to foster and encourage
artistic skill in the younger generation. These young
craftsmen show much natural skill only surpassed by

Leiderdorp, who is paying a 12-months visit to this
country to learn our methods and designs in the Pottery
craft. Herman hopes to take over the family pottery,
now being run by his father in Holland, which was
started by his grandfather.

activity: potter Miss Maisie Seneshall putting two of her cat models into the kiln for firing at her Kensington pottery

te.text:
PUSS POTTER.
MJH/MJH.
As she works in her pottery at Kensington (W. London),
Miss Maisie Seneshall is surrounded by cats of all sizes,
all colours, all breeds and in a variety of poses, but there
is never a purr or a mew.  For these cats are now real, they
are the result of Miss Seneshall's skill as a potter, for
she specialises in pottery cats, finding a ready market for
this work both in this country and overseas.  Miss
Seneshall's models are "true to life" for she sketches cats
in various poses at Cat Shows, etc, to give authenticity to her
work.
PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS:  MISS MAISIE SENESHALL seen putting two
of her cat models - a Siamese and a tabby - into the kiln
for firing at her Kensington (W. London) pottery.

FORGE MAY GO AFTER 90 YEARS.               AH/RS.

Master Farrier, George Banning of Balls Pond Road, Dalston,
may have to retire. At his address is the only forge in the
District, which has been in the family nearly 90 years. All
buildings where the forge now stands are to be demolished
and Mr. Banning may have to open up business elsewhere.
More than 100 horses a week go to him to be shod. These
come mostly from tradesman and Riding Schools in the Home
Counties. His assistant Bill Turner aged 50, has also been
in the business since his youth.

Photo Shows- Mr. George Banning 67 yrs, (RIGHT) with the assistance
of Bill Turner, shoeing a horse, at his forge at Balls Pond
Road.

Mr. T.O.M. Sopwith's America's Cup challenger Endeavour is

is enthusiastic about the new yacht. Endeavour is to be a

activity: View of the ship Tiger being dismantled in a ship breaking yard.

te.text:
WH
THE GRAVEYARD OF THE SEA GIANTS.
A remarkable sight meets the eye at the ship breaking yard
of Thomas Ward, Ltd, at Inverkeithing. Ships no longer look
like ships, rather do they resemble masses of old iron. It is
difficult to believe that ships like the Cedric and the Tiger
once the pride of their services could be reduced to their
present state in the short space of six weeks. But such is the
destructiveness of man, and shortly they will both be
reduced to their last bolt.
Photo shows- A general view of the Tiger in the hands of the
shipbreaker- a view that few Naval men would recognise as being
the famous Tiger.
FOX May/9th.32.

SUPPLIED BY
FOX PHOTOS LTD.
6, TUDOR STREET
LONDON, E.C.4.

te.text:
PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
--8 MAR 1962
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

ENGINE STRIPPED AFTER 100,000 MILES TEST
March 8th 1962 PAR XX94991-2 (Sa-G)

The engine of a Morris Mini-Minor
dismantled and laid out for inspection
at the BP Research Establishment at
Sunbury-on-Thames, Middlesex, to-day
(Thursday) at the end of a 100,000 miles
'static' motor oil proving trial for BP 'Visco-
static' motor oil.
MR. J. CLYDESALE, Foreman Mechanic,
is inspecting one of the parts. He was
responsible for all routine service
checks during the trial.
Six production cars, selected at random
from showrooms by the RAC, took part
in the test. They were a Ford Anglia,
Hillman Minx, 3.8 Jaguar, Morris Mini-
Minor, Triumph Herald 1200 and a
Vauxhall Velox. All successfully
completed the 100,000 miles, which
began on May 1st last year after all
the engines had been sealed.
Most of the driving was done on the
M 1 Motorway but the cars were also
taken on to town and country roads, and
hill climbs also featured in the trial.
The engines were stripped down under
RAC supervision at Sunbury-on-Thames.
March 8th 1962. PAR XX 94991-2 (Sa-G)

No reproduction fee:

Issued with the compliments of the
BRITISH PETROLEUM COMPANY
INDUS - MOTOR CAR - TESTING - RESEARCH - ETC

activity: Idle car assembly lines at the Rover Works due to coal shortages.

te.text:
SHORTAGE OF COAL BRINGS BRITAIN'S BIG INDUSTRY
TO STANDSTILL
- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
4-2-47

The big Midlands car factory, the Rover Works, Birmingham
has been paralysed owing to the coal shortage. Cars for
export and home market were being made here. Day by day they
moved off the production line, till coal stocks dwindled
to nothing, as consumption, even with every economy, out-
distanced supply. Like many other factories, these works
are paralysed by the coal shortage, and the plant stood
silent for three days.
I.N.P. PHOTO SHOWS: No coal - so the rotors stand idle
and no car has moved forward on
the assembly lines.

SPECIAL.
117/J. 6061
INTERNATIONAL NEWS PHOTOS

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE

date_info.rationale: This date is typed at the end of the news caption, indicating when the copy was prepared for dispatch.

activity: Men working on the spacious interior of the 'Brabazon's' main passenger cabin.

te.text:
126-TON 'BRABAZON' NEARS COMPLETION, WILL FLY THIS SUMMER.

Under the hands of 700 workers, the world's biggest landplane
is nearing completion at the plant of the Bristol Aeroplane
Company at Filton, Bristol.
Designed to be the aerial counterpart of the 'Queen Elizabeth' -
world's greatest ocean liner - the plane is the 'Brabazon I',
the gigantic sections of which are almost ready for final assembly.
It is expected that the 126-ton monster will take the air
for the first time in May or June and that three other
Brabazons on order will be flying on the London-New York service
of British Overseas Airways by 1950.
The Brabazon is a high-altitude, long-range low-wing cantilever
monoplane which will accommodate 70 to 100 sleeping passengers
or 120 sitting passengers in the utmost comfort.  The
143-feet cabin will be pressurised to maintain an equivalent
cabin altitude of 8,000 feet while flying at 25,000 feet.
Crew will number 13, including five stewards.
Wingspan of the aircraft is 230 feet - almost twice that
of Britain's largest bomber, the Avro Lincoln - and the height
over the rudder is 50 feet.
Eight Bristol 'Centaurus' 18-cylinder, sleeve-valve,
air-cooled radial engines, each rated at 2,500 brake horsepower
for take-off, will give a maximum level speed of more than 300
miles an hour at 25,000 feet, and economical cruising speed
of 250 miles an hour at the same altitude, and a still-air range
of 5,000 miles.  Initial service ceiling will be 25,000 feet,
increasing as fuel is consumed.
PHOTO SHOWS:- Men working on the spacious interior of the
'Brabazon's' main passenger cabin.
AND March 31st 1947 PN.r.

activity: combined harvester and wagon emptying grain in Alberta

te.text:
WONDERFUL LABOUR SAVING DEVICE USED IN
CANADIAN HARVESTING.

EIGHT THOUSAND BUSHELS PER DAY CUT AND THRASHED
BY ONE MACHINE WITHOUT BINDING AND STOOKING.

What is believed to have been the greatest use made of
mechanical power in farming ever witnessed in Western
Canada was used in the recent harvesting at Aldersyde
Alberta. A combined reaping and threshing machine was
used which dispenses with the idea of cutting in the
first place and the usual stooking by hand labour for
sun drying. This machine is used when the wheat
is dry and is out, thrown in the thresher and the wheat
transferred into a huge tank. When this is full the
wagons are brought up into which the wheat is again
transferred and then on to the elevator. The
importance of the invention is that it dispenses with
cutting and stooking, also solves the problem the
Western Farmers have experienced in getting
harvesters at the important moment. The success
has been so great it is considered it will not
be long before these machines are used universally.

Photo shows:- General view of the combined harvester
and wagon emptying the grain receptable to get it
ready for its next operation.

Note companion picture.

title: A photographic print of Home & Housing, Post War, Slums & Living Conditions (UK Wide)

date_info.rationale: Date 4/12/46 is likely 4 December 1946 given the UK format and the caption's explicit reference to 'cold weather'. April 12th is a secondary possibility.

activity: Mrs. Cropp and children at the door of their 'home', a wooden fruit picker's hut on Wested Farm.

te.text:
PROBLEM OF A WOMAN AND SIX CHILDREN
---
Living in one room - a wooden fruit picker's
hut, on Wested Farm, Crockenhill, near Swanley,
Kent, is Mrs. May Cropp, her three children and a
further three grandchildren (offspring of one of her
daughters).
She is a squatter. There is no sanitation
anywhere near the hut - nor the usual amenities. The
hut leaks, is unsanitary, and is certainly not
weather-
proof.
How she came to be there does not matter - what
does matter is that she cannot get another home to
live - and owing to the bad state of affairs the
farmer, C.T.Miller, of Wested Farm, has asked the
police to evict them in the hope that they will
be found better accomodation.
As it is, the children - ranging from a few
months to six years - cannot possibly be properly
fed, clothed and educated - and there is no talk of
them going regularly to school.
In this cold weather, some of them are to
be seen playing in the mud around their "home".
The Dartford Rural District Council, under
whose jurisdiction their "home" comes, should look
into the matter - the farmer is certainly not to
blame - it is the best housing he can offer - even
to squatters.
PICTURE SHOWS:
2. Mrs. Cropp and children at the door of their
"home".
19836   4/12/46   John Topham, Sidcup, Kent.

With the compliments of British Nylon Spinners Ltd.
Press Office: 68 Knightsbridge,
London, S.W.1.
KENsington 6333
HP 118428 & HP 118431
Built up to first floor height completely in the dry, this house at
Hampton, Middlesex was the first in Britain to be protected by a nylon
airhouse. Manufactured by The Gourock Ropework Co. Ltd., the vast "igloo" of
coated nylon fabric, measuring 70 ft. by 40 ft. by 20 ft., covered the entire
site. The structure is held up solely by a constant supply of low pressure
air and experience showed that one 5,000 cubic ft./minute electric fan, costing
less than twopence an hour to run, was adequate for the greater part of the
time. Only when constant traffic was going in and out of the doors was a
second fan necessary.

2020)   50 YEARS AS STAINED GLASS ARTIST

te.text: File / Industries - Fuel & Power - Oil Wells - British

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION TUESDAY'S EVENINGS, May 6th.
ENGLAND'S OILFIELD NOW PRODUCES IN MILLIONS
6.5.47.
Since 1939 England's only big-scale oilfield has produced more
than ten million gallons of oil, and the wells are now yielding
better than 150 tons a day. The field stretches for 100 square
miles beneath the "Dukeries" the name by which that area of the
English Midlands is known where so many of the premier peers have
their stately homes and family seats. This photograph was taken
at EAKRING, Nottinghamshire, where about 450 men are employed
by the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company. Oil is reached at about 2,000
feet. The typical British oil-man - LOFTY SANDERS, wearing pro-
tective headgear, holding the drill-bit which bits through the
rock and earth to reach the oil layer 2,000 feet below the ground.

THIS FILM IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

[illegible] ISSUED BY
[illegible] PHOTOS LTD.
[illegible]ations Service,
[illegible], LONDON, E.C.4

te.text:
SURVIVORS from the ill-fated oil
drilling rig Sea Gem, which col-
lapsed and sank in the North Sea
yesterday, told a story of Boxing Day
horror when they came ashore last
night.
All 32 men aboard the 5,600-ton, 10-legged rig
—which discovered a rich undersea gas field a
week ago—were plunged
into the sea when the
whole structure mys-
teriously capsized, 40
miles off Grimsby.
Late last night 20
men — some of them
injured—were known to
have survived. Three
men were picked up
dead from the icy water
and nine men were
missing.
Most of the survivors
were landed at Hull by the
2,000-ton British ship
Baltrover.
They told of the last few
minutes they spent on the
platform of the huge rig,
which was operated by
British Petroleum.

KEITH JOHNSON
RED LION COURT

LONDON [illegible]

activity: Prototype houses constructed via the 5M industrialised building system.

te.text:
CROWN COPYRIGHT RESERVED. MINISTRY OF HOUSING & LOCAL GOVERNMENT.
Four prototype houses built for the Sheffield City Council by the
Public Works Department under the 5M system of construction devised
by the Research and Development Group of the Ministry of Housing
and Local Government. This system, which marks a new attempt to
bring the advantages of industrialisation into the field of house-
building, has been derived from the 5M CLASP system used at
Stevenage for a group of old people's flatlets. The new system
is called 5M, because as at Stevenage, it is based upon a planning
grid of 1' 8" (5 x the module of 4"). The object has been to
modify the CLASP system which has been shown to have advantages in
the reduction of site labour and building time, to suit the
performance standards, and the levels of cost, of 2-storey housing.
Ministry of Housing & Local Government. January, 1963

NOT TO BE PUBLISHED BEFORE THURSDAY'S
DAILIES 8TH FEBRUARY, 1962.

FIRST VICKERS VC 10 IS NEARING COMPLETION
ODS 7.2.62.
THE FIRST VICKERS VC 10 LONG-RANGE JET AIRLINER
IS NOW STRUCTURALLY ALMOST COMPLETE AND SYSTEM
AND FLIGHT TEST EQUIPMENT ARE BEING INSTALLED
AT THE VICKERS-ARMSTRONGS (AIRCRAFT) WORKS AT
WEYBRIDGE, SURREY. THE VC 10, THE FIRST BIG JET
AIRLINER WITH REAR-MOUNTED ENGINES, IS SCHEDULED
TO MAKE ITS FIRST FLIGHT IN MAY.
THE VC 10 IS THE BIGGEST SINGLE AIRCRAFT
PROJECT EVER TACKLED IN EUROPE. WITH ITS FOUR
ADVANCED-MODEL ROLLS-ROYCE CONWAY ENGINES IT WILL
BE THE WORLD'S MOST POWERFUL AIRLINER (ALTHOUGH
[crossed out] NOISE PROBLEMS WILL NOT BE INCREASED DUE
TO THE BETTER TAKE-OFF AND CLIMB PERFORMANCE OF THE
CLEAN-WINGED VC 10; IN FACT, IT WILL BE LESS
RESTRICTED BY AIRPORT NOISE REGULATIONS THAN CURRENT
BIG JETS). THE VC 10 CRUISES AT UP TO 600 M.P.H. ITS
MAXIMUM RANGE WITH 100 PASSENGERS AND RESERVES IS
OVER 5,000 MILES, OF 4,400 MILES WITH FULL PAY-LOAD.
ORDERS HAVE BEEN ANNOUNCED FOR 54 VC 10s -
42 FOR BOAC, FIVE FOR RAF TRANSPORT COMMAND, FOUR
FOR BRITISH UNITED AIRWAYS AND THREE FOR GHANA
AIRWAYS.

GATHERING THE NORFOLK REED HARVEST. 		AW/FM

Reed thatching in England is one of the most ancient crafts,
and the craft is reviving. The reeds come mostly from the
Norfolk Broads, where great quantities are harvested about
this time of the year, when the leaves are gone. Cutting
lasts until the young shoots appear in early April. These
reeds are used for thatching principally but are also used
for making large fish and fruit baskets, known as Skeps.

ROPER.   14.1.38.
BUNNY THE CART HORSE ESCAPES.
When an outdoor film sequence was made
this morning at Alexandra Palace, Bunny
the carthorse threw his rider, who was
King Marke, and escaped. The King's
knights and bodyguard chased Bunny all
over the Palace grounds and eventually
captured him, but film work was held
up for an hour. The film will be
merged into [crossed-out text] hunting scenes
to be interpolated in the television
transmission of "Tristan und Isolade",
on January 24. The actual chase seen
in this photograph will be televised
during the overture.

activity: Promotional release for Cormar Hi-Twist carpets featuring Courtaulds fibres.

te.text:
PRESS OFFICE,
22 Hanover Square,
London W.1.
TELEPHONE: MAYfair 8000

Carpets with a high twist pile are ever gaining in popularity as people
discover the advantages of a crush-resistant pile which shows no marks
of shading or scuffing. The twist in the fibre not only gives a beautiful
textured effect to a plain carpet: it also ensures that the pile is much
harder wearing.

Greenwood and Coope were the first to realise the advantages of man-made
fibres in twist pile carpets when they produced Hi-Twist, the hard twist
carpet made of 50% Courtelle/50% Evlan. This blend of Courtaulds fibres
is particularly suitable for a twist pile carpet: the thermoplastic
qualities of Courtelle mean that the twist in the pile can be set by heat,
just like the pleats in a skirt, and this twist is permanent.

Hi-Twist presents very few problems where soiling and cleaning are concerned.
The presence of Evlan in the carpet prevents any electrostatic charge
building up - it is this charge that attracts particles of dirt in acrylic
fibres. Even when normal domestic accidents occur and the carpet is stained,
it is no problem to clean because the Courtelle in the carpet means that it
shampoos beautifully and dries very quickly.

Kinky pile carpets not only look good - they also wear much better, and
so Hi-Twist, of course, qualifies for Courtaulds Extra Duty Label which
means that it can be used for any location in the home.

At 52/6d a square yard it is very good value for money.

For further information:
Miss Alexa Smith,
Ext. 347.

activity: Casting and spinning iron pipes in a British ironworks for utility services.

te.text:
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION FRIDAY'S EVENINGS DECEMBER 19th.

SPINNING THE ARTERIES OF OUR CIVILISATION. 19.12.41.
This is one of a remarkable new series of photographs
taken mainly by the natural light of the processes
by which a British ironworks produce mile upon mile
of cast iron pipes for the public services of gas and
water which are prime necessity of civilised life.
A large percentage of these pipes are spun by a centrifugal
process which eliminates defects and gives a close-
grained metal, easily worked and with a high degree
of resilience and resistance to impact. In addition
to its own requirements, the plant also produces
pig-iron for steel manufacture, contributing largely
therefore to the country's output of armaments.
Blast furnace hand waiting to commence tapping.

te.text:
PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
REC'D 11 AUG 1954
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

PEER TO VISIT PIT GIRLS. MJH/VIG.

In reply to a challenge by Viscount Hall, arising out of
controversy over the second reading of the Mines and Quarries
Bill in the House of Lords, the Earl of Selkirk (Paymaster
General) is to spend part of his holiday touring collieries
to "see for himself" conditions under which the "pit brow
lassies" work. Viscount Hall declared that there were about
1,000 women still employed at the pit tops working in conditions
almost as bad as those prevailing at the time, when women
were taken out of the pits nearly 100 years ago.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS: 18-years-old JOAN HOLGATE, youngest member
of her shaft seen employed on the cleaning of coal at the
Bickershaw Colliery, Leigh, near Manchester. She gave up
the cleaner job of waitress to work at the pit head and is quite
happy in her work. The "pit brow lassies" work an eight-hour
shift and say that, although the work is very dirty, it is
quite congenial. A modern bath-house is provided for their
use and protective clothing is also provided.
FOX PHOTOS AUGUST 9TH. 1954. 502722.

te.text:
KING AND QUEEN TO VISIT CORNISH CLAY INDUSTRY
WILL SEE ST. AUSTELL PIT

When the King and Queen visit the West Country at the end
of October, they will inspect the china clay factory at
St. Austell, Cornwall, where the industry of china clay
digging has been carried on for 130 years.
The valuable raw material is still being mined and exported
in increasing quantities for use in drugs, cosmetics,
paper, paint, rubber and pottery making.
The white hills which surround the Lower Ninestones Pit at
St. Austell, are often spoken of as the Cornish "Alps", as a
result of the sand which is transported from the pits, and
deposited at the tops.
PHOTO SHOWS:- This joined photograph shows a clear view
of the 200 foot deep Lower Ninestones Pit, from top
to bottom.

The hosing of clay down the side of the pit can be seen
on the left, while at the bottom, are the purifying pits
and the trolleys which take the remains to the top by
railway.
MD Oct 23rd 1947 PN g

PRINTED CIRCUIT TRANSISTORS? TO REDUCE SIZE OF "ELECTRONIC 
BRAINS" ANNOUNCED BY DEPART OF THE U.S. ARMY.

                  Printed circuit transistors, developed
by the U.S. Army research scientist DR.J.W. LATHROP, will
greatly reduce the size of many items of military equipment
including the electronic brain of guided missile aircraft.
Use of the printed circuit method produces a transistor
about 1/20th. of an inch wide and 1,100th. of an inch high
and provides increased reliability and resistance to shock or 
vibration. It is expected that some equipment can be reduced
to one tenth of their present sizes through use of the new 
transistor to control the flow of current in electronic
circuits. Dr. Lathrop is scientist with the Army's Diamond
Fuse Laboratories, Washington, D.C.. Small "dot" on board
upper left is the new transistor, compared in size to the

activity: part of the world's largest banqueting service, ordered by the government of Ghana and completed by John Aynsley pottery firm

te.text:
PROPERTY 
 SUN 
 13 JUL 1966 
 Please return to 
 ART LIBRARY

THIS ROOMFUL of china is only part of the world's largest banqueting service. It was ordered by the government of Ghana and has just been completed by John Aynsley, a Stoke-on-Trent pottery firm. 
 Unfortunately the former president, Nkrumah, was deposed after his personal crest had been engraved on many of the pieces. The crest had to be rubbed out by the firm's craftsmen. 
 It's a good thing the service had not all been engraved; altogether there were over 18,000 pieces, from meat dishes to coffee cups. 
 The service was made in three stages. In 1960 4,800 pieces were turned out, in 1963 another 6,600 and now the last 7,000 have been completed. 
 Michael Gillow, the firm's managing director, says: "Removing the crest was a very tricky operation, but we have managed it." 
 Now the world's biggest banqueting service is strictly anonymous.

te.text:
AN UNUSUAL JOB                      MJH/FM.

The unusual "line" of Mrs. Mollie Surman of Kingston
(Surrey) is making glass eyes - a very skilled craft
which she learned from her father the late Mr. G. Taylor.
Mrs. Surman, who believes she is one of the only two
women glass-eye blowers in the country, first started
to learn this craft during her school holidays at the
age of 12 and to date, she estimates that she has made
about 12,000-to 15,000 eyes.  This has been a family
craft for about 160 years. Mrs. Surman's grandfather
made glass eyes for the 2nd. Duke of Wellington, while
her father once made an artificial eye for a pedigree
Chow dog which won 1st. Prize at Crufts.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS:  Blonde 38-years-old MRS. MOLLIE SURMAN
seen at work in her Kingston studio on the skilled craft
of blowing a glass eye.  It takes her about 2 hours
to make an eye.

te.text:
Esten  D.H.  3.4.44
EPSOM PREPARES FOR OPENING OF RACING SEASON
Racing opens at Windsor on Easter Monday and trainers hope that it will be the last wartime season. Victor Smythe of Epsom has 48 horses in training this year, 35 of them untried 2-year olds. The increase is mainly due to a greater allocation of feeding stuffs, but labour is still a problem. Vic Smythe solves this by being assisted by part-time local labour to assist in riding and gallops. One of these is an Irish nurse from a local hospital who rides the horses in gallops with as much nerve as her professional colleagues.
OPS 1 Vic Smythe (on left) supervises a string consisting of 2-year olds.  He hopes the Derby will be run on his home ground next year.

activity: A team of international testers assessing a gas strike at a gas well in a field on a farm in South Godstone.

te.text:
ARTHUR STEEL SUN 3.1.66 
In a field at South Godstone a gas well and a team of testers. 
O.P.S. L. to R... Jean Cros (Beziers), Phillipe Neyron (Beziers), John 
Trewhella (Cornwall) Chief, Ken Atwood (Houston, Texas) engineer from Esso, 
and Jan Groenestein from Amsterdam.

FARMER John Collard tended his
cattle and sheep as usual yester-
day. He was philosophical about
the men ploughing through the
mud in his bottom field—even
though they have struck gas.
Said Mr. Collard: "It won't make
much difference to me even if large
quantities of the gas are found."
He's right, too. For in Britain all
mineral rights are vested in the Crown
(which means, in this case, the Ministry
of Power).
The prospectors, too, were philo-
sophical about their strike on the
Collards' 200-acre farm at South
Godstone, Surrey.
Cornishman John Trewhella, who now
lives at Alkmaar in Holland, said:
"Optimistic? That's too strong a word.
We're just hopeful."
Mr. Trewhella, who
heads the team of con-
tractors called in to assess
the quality and quantity
of the strike, said: "We
will be testing for a week
or 10 days. Then we
should know how much
gas is here."
STRIKE
The search for gas down
on the farm began long
before the North Sea hunt.
The Esso Petroleum Com-
pany were granted prospect-
ing licences six years ago.
They negotiated agreements
with landowners in Hampshire,
Sussex, Kent and Surrey—and
began drilling four years ago.
From Mr. Collard they rented
a field on Langham Park Farm
where villagers had played foot-
ball for nearly 40 years.
And it was there that Esso
scored with an international
team captained by 37-year-old
Ken Atwood, of Houston, Texas.
Working with him and Mr.
Trewhella are Dutch and
French drilling experts.
Their strike is just off the
main London-Eastbourne road
—23 miles from London—oppo-
site Gus Rossini's transport
café.
GUSHER
Mr. Rossini said last night:
"When the gas is gushing, it's
lit. And the flames reach 30ft.
high or more. Then it's like a
fairground round here."
Friends who don't know about
mineral rights optimistically tell
Farmer Collard: "You'll be a
millionaire..."
But with an appropriate agri-
cultural turn of phrase, Mr.
Collard commented: "They're
counting my chickens before
they are hatched."
Brightening, he added: "We
must get a private pipeline.
After all, we cook with gas."

BRITISH OFFICIAL PHOTOGRAPH NO. T.29 (WN).
MINISTRY OF FUEL AND POWER) CROWN COPYRIGHT

OPERATION PLUTO (PIPE LINES UNDER THE OCEAN)
FIRST PICTURES.
One of the greatest supply stories of the war is now
being told for the first time. It is the story of
Operation "Pluto" (from the initial letters of
"Pipe Lines Under The Ocean") It tells of the laying
by unique methods of an oil pipe line system under
the Englsih Channel by which the Miliarty operations
of the Allied Armies in Europe were noursshed. This
system was devised by the Petroleum Warfare Dept.
and its success owes much to the Prime Minister's
interest.
(These photo shows tie up with the Ministry of
Fuel and Power Press Conference on Tuesday May 22nd.
Picture shows. Drums for carrying steel pipe were
known as "Conuns" (H.M.S. Conundrums). This picture
shows a Conun being towed by the Royal Navy across
the Channel and laying the first continuous length
of stee pipe 67 miles long.

MUST NOT BE PUBLISHED BEFORE 00.30. HOURS THURSDAY
MAY 24th. I.E. FOR THURSDAY MORNING PAPERS.

SET OF APOSTLE SPOONS OFFERED FOR SALE-AT CHRISTIES
BOUGHT-IN AT £6,200..

           A complete set of very rare
Elizabethan Apostle Spoons - property of MR. JAMES
MABON of New York - were offered for sale at Christies
this morning - and were 'bought in' for £6,200. The
spoons - known as the 'Frith Set' - because they
were once owned by the Victorian Squire Frith of
Bank Hall, Derbyshire. There are thirteen spoons in
an 'Apostle' set - one for each apostle and on e
"Master" or Christ spoon. Twelve of the Frith spoons
bear the hallmark 1592 - the thirteenth spoon is
somewhat later.

KEYSTONE PHOTO SHOWS:- The set of FRITH APOSTLE

FOR WEDNESDAY'S DAILIES
CLYDE YARD COMPLETED FIRST OF LARGEST BRITISH TANKERS.
JS. 10.12.52.
Now nearing completion in readiness for the launching
ceremony on December 17th at Messrs John Brown's shipyard
on the Clyde, is the 32,000-ton tanker "BRITISH SAILOR"
the first of seven similar sized tankers for the British
Tanker Company. The vessel will be the largest oil tanker
ever launched on the Clyde, and will be the largest British
owned tanker sailing the seas. Nearby in the same yard a
start has been made on the second tanker, the "BRITISH
SOLDIER" and they will make a valuable addition to the
British Tanker Company's fleet bringing oil from the Middle
East to the refineries in Britain. This is one of a series
taken illustrating their construction, and shows:-

te.text:
THE ROYAL SHOW  1963.                PC/

The Royal Show 1963 is taking place at
Stoneleigh Abbey Park, near Kenilworth,
Warwickshire.  For nearly one hundred
and twenty five years the Royal Show has
been taking place annually in various
parts of the country - it has now returned
to the Midlands to Stoneleigh Abbey, the
seat of Lord Leigh, which is hoped will
become its permanent site.  During the
many years the show has been taking place,
a great deal of changes have been made
to its presentation - and this years new
feature is the helicopter service from
which visitors can get an overall view
of the enormous area covered by the show
rings and exhibition stands. During the
build-up for the show the extremely bad
and wet weather has caused much havoc
but thanks to the herculean efforts made
by all concerned the show will go on as
usual. H.M.Queen Elizabeth II and the
Duke of Edinburgh, (President of the Royal
Agricultural Society of England this year)
will visit the show on Thursday, 4th. They
are expected to enter the main ring in a
carriage drawn by Windsor Greys.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS:-   An aerial view of
the Royal Show, at Stoneleigh Abbey Park,
Warwickshire, to-day, Monday.

FIRST DROPS OF A NEW WINE
Nov 14th 1956 PAR 60018-1 (Wo-J)


FIRST DROPS OF A NEW WINE

Assistant 'vigneron' ERNEST BLACKMAN holds a
jug to catch the first drops being squeezed
from the press by Sir GUY SALISBURY-JONES,
Marshal of the Diplomatic Corps, pressing
grapes for a new wine at his country home at
Hambledon, Hampshire.
Watching are LADY SALISBURY-JONES, their son
RAYMOND and daughter MARIETTE.
The wine, to be named 'Hambledon', will be
matured by next July and placed on the market
in time for Christmas next year.
The vineyard at Hambledon is in its fifth year
but grapes from younger vines are not good
enough for wine.  Sir Guy bottled some of
last year's crop for his own use this
Christmas but it will not be sold.
Despite bad weather this year, the grapes have
exceeded expectations at Hambledon and are in
better condition than those at many of the
famous French vineyards.
Nov 14th 1956 PAR 60018-1 (Wo-J)

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION IN EVENING PAPERS OF 
THURSDAY NOVEMBER 15th 1956

activity: squaring through a length of netting with a knife

te.text:
THE MODERN GIRL PLIES A CENTURIES-OLD TRADE
July 13th 1953 PAR 36404 -2 (BKS-R)
_________________________________________________________
THE MODERN GIRL PLIES A CENTURIES-OLD TRADE

For at least seven centuries, the manufacture
of nets, ropes, sailcloth and other hempen
products has been the staple industry of
the town of Bridport, Dorset.
Of Bridport's present-day population of about
6,000, over a thousand - many of them young
women - are engaged in the industry,
directly or indirectly.
At one time locally-grown flax and hemp were
used, but nearly all the raw material is
now imported.
It is recorded that all the ropes and sails
for King John's Navy (he reigned from
1199-1216) were made at Bridport. And the
expression 'stabbed by a Bridport dagger' for
a person who had been hanged was current
in 1530, when King Henry VIII reigned.
This picture was taken in the Bridport works
of Joseph Gundry and Co. Ltd., a firm founded
in 1665 and still controlled by lineal
descendants of the founder. There were
Gundrys engaged in the trade as early as 1580.
PICTURE SHOWS:- PHYLLIS STROUD, attractive
representative of modern Bridport,
'squaring through' a length of netting
with a knife.
July 13th 1953 PAR 36404-2 (BKS-R)

activity: 70 year old blacksmith Nathaniel Barber at his forge at Milford Mill

te.text:
ESTEN    D.H.    1.2.44.
NAT'S SCORE IS 25,000 not out.
In the tiny hamlet of Milford situated on the
outskirts of Salisbury lives 70 year old Nathaniel
Barber, Blacksmith for 53 years. Nat belongs to
a fast dying profession, for blacksmiths are now
becoming a rarity.
Motor Engineer is the new term for where Nat used
to shoe over 200 horses six times a year, now only
20 come to him to be reshod.
Nat's father was a blacksmith as were four of his
eight brothers of whom he is the only one left.
In spite of the lack of horses to shoe, Nat
persuaded his 40 year old son to learn the craft
and now when Nat passes on, Ronald will become the
fourth generation of Barber - Blacksmith.
Nat boasts of the time he shood famous racehorses
in the district.
Nat estimates that he has made and forged 25,000
shoes in his 53 years and hopes to make a few more
thousand yet. He works from dawn till dusk six
days a week throughout the year.
There is another son, Horace, profession motor
engineer.
O.P.S.1    70 year old Nat. Barber at the forge
           at Milford Mill.

activity: Elizabeth Greenhill bookbinding in her Essex Street workshop.

te.text:
ANCIENT CRAFT IN MODERN LONDON.
WOMAN BOOKBINDER WORKS ON HISTORIC SITE.

An ancient handicraft is being carried
on in a basement in Essex Street, within
earshot of the bustling Strand, by
Miss Elizabeth Greenhill, the bookbinder.
Miss Greenhill has opened a new workshop
in the house which used to be the old
water-gate to Essex House in the days when
it was the palace of Robert Devereux,
Earl of Essex, and favourite of Queen
Elizabeth.
Miss Greenhill first achieved fame in her
craft when she bound "The Gloucester Bible",
the personal gift of Mr. Leslie Boyce, M.P.
to Gloucester City to commemorate the
jubilee of King George V.
She has just completed a special binding
for a copy of "Pride and Prejudice" for
Queen Mary, and another book for Princess
Margaret Rose.
PHOTO SHOWS:- Miss Elizabeth Greenhill busy
in her workshop at the foot of Essex Stairs,
Essex Street.
GAIC September 29th 1937 PN-r.

COPYRIGHT.
PLANET NEWS LTD
3, JOHNSON'S COURT,
LONDON, E.C. 4.
