te.text:
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION IN DAILIES
OF FRIDAY 9TH OCTOBER 1964.

NORTH SEA GEOPHYSICAL OPERATIONS.
ERF. G. OCTOBER 1964
BRITISH PETROLEUM HAS BEEN AWARDED PRODUCTION
LICENCES BY THE MINISTRY OF POWER, COVERING
SOME 2,200 SQUARE MILES IN AREA, TO SEARCH FOR
AND PRODUCE OIL AND NATURAL GAS UNDER THE
NORTH SEA ADJACENT TO THE UNITED KINGDOM. THE
AREAS LIE OFF THE COAST OF DURHAM, YORKSHIRE
AND LINCOLNSHIRE.
THE COMPANY HAS DRAWN UP PLANS FOR
ITS OWN SUBSTANTIAL DRILLING PROGRAMME. THE
B.P. AREA HAS BEEN DIVIDED INTO THREE PRODUCTION
LICENCES, IN EACH OF WHICH ONE DEEP TEST WILL
INITIALLY BE DRILLED; THE PROGRAMME FOR FURTHER
TEST DRILLING WILL BE DRAWN UP AS DICTATED BY
EXPERIENCED IT IS EXPECTED THAT EACH WELL WILL BE
ABOUT 12,000 FEET IN DEPTH AND WILL COST AT LEAST
£500,000. DRILLING OPERATIONS WILL COMMENCE
AS EARLY AS PRACTICABLE IN 1965. GEOPHYSICAL
WORK HAS ALREADY BEGUN IN ORDER TO AID SELECTION
OF DRILLING LOCATIONS.
PHOTO SHOWS:
ON BOARD THE SURVEY VESSEL "TEXIN" - SIGNALS
FROM EACH SHOCK WAVE, WHICH APART FROM BEING
RECORDED ON TAPE, ( [illegible] ), ARE PHOTOGRAPHICALLY
REPRODUCED AS AN IMMEDIATE VISUAL CHECK.
THE EFFECT OF THE SHOCK WAVES ARE RELAYED BY THE
"STREAMER" FROM THE DEPTH CHARGES ECHOED FROM
THE ROCK FORMATION BELOW THE SEA BED.
THE "STREAMER" IS RUN OUT ASTERN
OF THE SHIP AND IS SOMETIMES WELL OVER A MILE
LONG.
G.10014

H.M. the King was represented by Princess Elizabeth
at today's Birthday Trooping of the Colours at the

te.text:
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION WEDNESDAY'S EVENINGS, Oct 2nd.

SEA PLANES WILL SEEK WHALES FOR FLOATING FACTORY
                                          2.10.46.
The United Whalers' 15000-ton factory ship BALAENA, first of
its kind to be fitted with aircraft for whale-spotting and
weather reconnaissance, has been handed over to her owners
after trials in Belfast Lough, and will shortly leave for
the Antarctic in search of badly needed whale oil.
The ship will carry three converted Walrus amphibian air-
craft which will be launched from a double-acting catapult
working on a cordite charge, or lowered over the side for a
normal take-off by the crane which also lifts them from the
water after a flight.
The BALAENA will act as mother ship for a fleet of about ten
whale-catchers, and her factory contains one of the largest
oil-producing plants ever installed in a ship, and elaborate
machinery for dealing with by-products; refrigerating gear
will freeze the choicest parts of the whale meat for human
consumption.   The picture shows
A close-view of the stern and flight-deck of the
BALAENA, showing one of the amphibian Walruses and the
crane, and the aperture through which the whales are
hauled up into the factory.

COPYRIGHT PHOTO ISSUED BY
CENTRAL PRESS PHOTOS LTD.
INCORPORATING
Central News Illustrations Service,
119, FLEET STREET, LONDON, E.C.4

te.text:
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION EVENING PAPERS THURDAY NOV. 6th.

SPINNING THE ARTERIES OF OUR CIVILISATION
6. 11. 41.
This is one of a remarkable new series of photo-
hraphs taken mainly by the natural light of the
processes by which a British ironworks produces
mile upon mile of cast iron pipes for the public
services of gas and water which are prime
necessity of civilised life. A large percentage
of these pipes are spun by a centrifugal process
which eliminates defects and gives a close-grained
metal, easily worked and with a high degree of
resilience and resistance to impact. In addition
to its own requirements, the plant also produces
pig-iron for steel manufacture, contributing
largely therefore to the country's output of
armaments.

operation.

activity: Transferring graded eels into floating containers alongside a barge.

te.text:
DAILY HERALD ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

1,000,000, EELS.
LIVE IN A BARGE FULL OF HOLES          DG/FM

Believed to be the first of its kind ever to
be built in this country, and certainly the
first of this particular design, the eel barge
"Johan", is literally a ship full of holes.
The centre part of the barge is perforated so that
water can be allowed to flow freely into it.
Watertight compartments support the barge, fore and
aft, and the deck is no more than 18 inches above
water level. The owner is Mr H. G. Kuitjen,
an importer of live eels. The eels come from
the seas between Norway and Corsica, and they are
brought by boat from the Continent.
The eels usually arrive in the autumn and are
graded by size into separate compartments. From
the barge they are packed into wet boxes for
Billingsgate. It is estimated that the barge
will 120,000 lbs of live eels- the shipping of
this 50 ton cargo will not increase the draught
draught of the vessel as the cargo is waterborne.

PHOTO SHOWS:- The graded eels are transferred into
floating containers alongside the barge at Heybridge
Basin, Malden, Essex. These are also floating
perforated containers.
